content: Hippocrates, who lived between 460 and 370 BC, was the first to describe the phenomenon of sudden paralysis, which he referred to as apoplexy. The term apoplexy originates from a Greek word meaning struck down with violence. This term appeared in Hippocratic writings to describe the condition. By 1599, the word stroke was being used as a synonym for apoplectic seizure, serving as a fairly direct translation of the Greek term. In 1658, Johann Jacob Wepfer, in his work titled Apoplexia, identified the cause of hemorrhagic stroke. He proposed that individuals who had died of apoplexy had experienced bleeding in their brains. Wepfer also identified the primary arteries supplying the brain, specifically the vertebral and carotid arteries. Furthermore, he suggested that apoplexy could also result from blockages in these vessels, thereby identifying the cause of ischemic stroke. In the United States, stroke is a leading cause of serious, long-term disability. Over the years, the incidence and mortality rates of stroke have significantly decreased. Between 2003 and 2013, mortality rates due to stroke declined by 18.5%. By 2013, stroke had become the fifth leading cause of death in the country. The case fatality rate for stroke is estimated to be 41.7 deaths per 100,000 people. Annually, approximately 795,000 people experience a stroke, with 610,000 being new cases and 185,000 being recurrent strokes. This translates to an incidence rate of 250 cases per 100,000 people. On average, one stroke occurs every four seconds, and one death from stroke occurs every four minutes. About 87% of all strokes are ischemic in nature. The economic burden of stroke in the United States is substantial, with an estimated annual cost of $34 billion. Globally, the World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that 15 million people experience a stroke each year. Of these, 5 million die, and another 5 million are left permanently disabled. Stroke can occur across all age groups, but its incidence is lower in individuals under the age of 40. The risk of stroke increases with advancing age. According to the WHO, approximately 8% of children with sickle cell disease experience a stroke. In 2009, 34% of individuals hospitalized for stroke were younger than 65 years old. Among people aged 18 to 50 years, the incidence of stroke is estimated to be around 10%. Mortality rates from stroke have declined across all age groups, with the following reductions observed: For individuals over 65 years of age, mortality rates decreased from 534.1 to 245.2 per 100,000. For those aged 45 to 65 years, rates declined from 43.5 to 20.2 per 100,000. For individuals aged 18 to 44 years, rates dropped from 3.7 to 2.0 per 100,000. Men have a higher incidence of stroke compared to women. Additionally, racial disparities exist in stroke risk and outcomes. African Americans are twice as likely to experience a first stroke compared to white individuals and have higher mortality rates. The stroke risk for Hispanic individuals falls between that of white and African American populations. Geographically, the incidence and mortality rates of stroke are higher in developing countries compared to developed nations. This disparity is attributed to factors such as lower socioeconomic status and limited access to healthcare facilities. Within the United States, the southeastern region has the highest death rates from stroke.
